sections.name: The Cell and Biomolecules of Life

questions.q: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion?
o: Golgi apparatus
rough endoplasmic reticulum
lysosome
nucleolus
questions.x: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the RER, modifies them (for example by glycosylation), and packages them into secretory vesicles. The RER makes the proteins; the nucleolus makes rRNA.

questions.q: Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
o: ribosomes
nucleus
mitochondria
endoplasmic reticulum
questions.x: All cells have ribosomes for protein synthesis: 70S in prokaryotes and 80S in the eukaryotic cytoplasm. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.q: Which is the correct pathway for a secretory protein after it is made?
o: rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → cell surface membrane
Golgi apparatus → rough ER → secretory vesicle → cell surface membrane
rough ER → lysosome → Golgi apparatus → cell surface membrane
free ribosome → nucleus → Golgi apparatus → cell surface membrane
questions.x: Ribosomes on the RER make the protein into the ER lumen. Transport vesicles carry it to the Golgi, which packages it into secretory vesicles that fuse with the membrane (exocytosis).

questions.q: A mitochondrion 5 μm long appears 25 mm long in an electron micrograph. What is the magnification?
questions.x: Magnification = image size / actual size. Convert to the same unit: 25 mm = 25 000 μm, and 25 000 / 5 = ×5000.

questions.q: A cell has an unusually large amount of rough ER and many Golgi stacks. What is its most likely function?
o: secreting proteins, such as digestive enzymes
storing lipids
carrying out rapid aerobic respiration for muscle contraction
detoxifying drugs
questions.x: Rough ER makes proteins for export and the Golgi packages them, so a cell rich in both (such as a pancreatic acinar cell) secretes proteins. Drug detoxification and lipid synthesis involve smooth ER.

questions.q: Which bond links the glucose residues in amylose?
o: α(1→4) glycosidic bonds
β(1→4) glycosidic bonds
α(1→6) glycosidic bonds
peptide bonds
questions.x: Amylose is an unbranched chain of α-glucose joined by α(1→4) glycosidic bonds, which makes it coil into a helix. β(1→4) bonds are in cellulose; α(1→6) bonds form the branches in amylopectin and glycogen.

questions.q: Name the bond formed by condensation between a fatty acid and glycerol.
questions.x: The –COOH of the fatty acid condenses with an –OH of glycerol, releasing water and forming an ester bond. A triglyceride has three.

questions.q: Which feature of cellulose gives it high tensile strength?
o: Straight chains of β-glucose lie side by side and are held together by many hydrogen bonds, forming microfibrils.
Its α-glucose chains coil into compact helices.
It is highly branched, with many α(1→6) bonds.
Disulfide bonds cross-link its chains.
questions.x: Alternate β-glucose residues are inverted, so the chain is straight. Parallel chains form many hydrogen bonds with each other, bundling into strong microfibrils. Helices and branches describe starch and glycogen.

questions.q: Why is glycogen's highly branched structure an advantage for an animal?
o: It has many free ends, so enzymes can hydrolyse it quickly to release glucose.
Branching makes it soluble, so it can travel in the blood.
Branching lets it form hydrogen bonds with cellulose.
Its branches store more energy per gram than lipids.
questions.x: Each branch ends in a glucose that enzymes can remove, so many glucose molecules can be released at once when energy is needed. Glycogen is insoluble and stays in cells; lipids store more energy per gram.

questions.q: Which property of phospholipids allows them to form a bilayer in water?
o: Each molecule has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
They have three fatty acid tails that repel water.
They are polymers of glycerol linked by peptide bonds.
They are fully soluble in water.
questions.x: Phospholipids are amphipathic. In water the heads face the water on both sides while the tails point inwards, away from it, forming a bilayer. Three tails would make it a triglyceride.

questions.q: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide?
o: primary
secondary
tertiary
quaternary
questions.x: The primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by peptide bonds. It determines how the chain folds into its secondary and tertiary structures.

questions.q: Which bonds hold the α-helix and β-pleated sheet in shape?
o: hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the polypeptide backbone
disulfide bonds between cysteine R groups
ionic bonds between charged R groups
peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
questions.x: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds within the backbone. Disulfide, ionic and hydrophobic interactions between R groups belong to tertiary structure.

questions.q: How does a competitive inhibitor affect an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
o: It lowers the rate, but adding enough substrate still reaches the same maximum rate.
It lowers the maximum rate, however much substrate is added.
It permanently denatures the enzyme.
It binds to the substrate and changes its shape.
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. At high substrate concentration the substrate outcompetes it, so Vmax is unchanged (but more substrate is needed to reach it).

questions.q: Adding more substrate does not restore the rate of an inhibited enzyme. The inhibitor most likely:
o: binds to a site other than the active site and changes the active site's shape
has a shape similar to the substrate and binds to the active site
is hydrolysed by the enzyme
binds to the substrate rather than the enzyme
questions.x: A non-competitive inhibitor binds to an allosteric site, altering the shape of the active site. Substrate cannot displace it, so Vmax is lowered whatever the substrate concentration.

questions.q: In a pathway A → B → C → D, product D inhibits the first enzyme by binding to its allosteric site. What happens when D builds up?
o: Conversion of A to B slows, so less D is made: negative feedback.
Conversion of A to B speeds up, so D accumulates further.
Only the enzyme converting C to D is affected.
A is converted directly into D.
questions.x: This is end-product inhibition. Excess D switches off the first enzyme, which reduces flow through the whole pathway and saves resources. When D is used up, the inhibition is released.

questions.q: Above an enzyme's optimum temperature, why does its rate fall sharply?
o: Hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape and substrates no longer fit.
Peptide bonds are hydrolysed, so the enzyme breaks into amino acids.
Molecules move too fast to collide.
The substrate is denatured.
questions.x: Increased vibration breaks the weaker bonds that maintain tertiary structure. The active site loses its complementary shape: the enzyme is denatured. Peptide bonds stay intact.

questions.q: How does oxygen cross the cell surface membrane?
o: simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer
facilitated diffusion through channel proteins
active transport by carrier proteins
endocytosis
questions.x: O₂ is small and non-polar, so it passes directly through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer, down its concentration gradient. No protein or ATP is needed.

questions.q: Glucose enters red blood cells down its concentration gradient through a specific carrier protein, without using ATP. What is this process?
o: facilitated diffusion
simple diffusion
active transport
osmosis
questions.x: Glucose is large and polar, so it needs a carrier (GLUT1). Moving down its gradient without ATP is facilitated diffusion.

questions.q: What is the role of cholesterol in animal cell membranes?
o: It regulates fluidity: it restrains phospholipid movement when warm and stops tight packing when cold.
It acts as a receptor for hormones.
It forms channels for ions.
It makes the membrane permeable to water.
questions.x: Cholesterol sits between phospholipid tails. It reduces fluidity at higher temperatures and prevents the tails packing and solidifying at low temperatures, buffering membrane fluidity.

questions.q: A plant cell with a water potential of −400 kPa is placed in a solution of −600 kPa. What happens?
o: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, and the cell may plasmolyse.
Water enters the cell, and it becomes turgid.
There is no net movement of water.
Solutes move into the cell by osmosis.
questions.x: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential: from the cell (−400) to the solution (−600). The protoplast shrinks and may pull away from the wall.

questions.q: For each ATP hydrolysed, what does the Na⁺/K⁺ pump move?
o: 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell
2 Na⁺ out of the cell and 3 K⁺ into the cell
3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out of the cell
1 Na⁺ out of the cell and 1 K⁺ into the cell
questions.x: The pump exports 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP, both against their gradients. This unequal exchange helps make the inside of the cell negative.

questions.q: Root hair cells are treated with cyanide, which stops aerobic respiration. Which process is most reduced?
o: uptake of mineral ions against their concentration gradient
uptake of water by osmosis
diffusion of CO₂ out of the cells
diffusion of O₂ into the cells
questions.x: Active transport needs ATP, which comes mainly from aerobic respiration. Osmosis and diffusion are passive and continue without ATP.

questions.q: Name the stage of mitosis in which chromosomes line up at the equator of the spindle.
questions.x: In metaphase, spindle fibres attached to the kinetochores align the chromosomes on the metaphase plate.

questions.q: A diploid cell contains 20 pg of DNA in G1. How much DNA is in each cell at the end of meiosis II?
o: 10 pg
5 pg
20 pg
40 pg
questions.x: S phase doubles it to 40 pg. Meiosis I separates homologues: 20 pg per cell. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids: 10 pg per cell, half the G1 amount.

questions.q: When and between which structures does crossing over occur?
o: prophase I, between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
prophase I, between sister chromatids of the same chromosome
metaphase II, between non-homologous chromosomes
anaphase I, between sister chromatids
questions.x: Homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) in prophase I. Chiasmata form between non-sister chromatids, which exchange sections. Swapping between identical sister chromatids would produce no new combinations.

questions.q: An organism has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment produce?
questions.x: 2n = 8 means n = 4 homologous pairs. Each pair can line up two ways in metaphase I, so there are 2⁴ = 16 combinations.

questions.q: A cell is heterozygous, Aa. A crossover happens between gene A and the centromere. When do alleles A and a separate into different cells?
o: anaphase II
anaphase I
prophase I
telophase I
questions.x: After the crossover each homologue has one A chromatid and one a chromatid. Anaphase I separates homologues, so each cell still has both alleles. They separate only when sister chromatids part in anaphase II.

questions.q: Which statement about tumour suppressor genes is correct?
o: Cancer usually needs loss-of-function mutations in both alleles.
A gain-of-function mutation in one allele is enough to cause uncontrolled division.
They code for growth factors that stimulate the cell cycle.
Their normal products speed up passage through cell cycle checkpoints.
questions.x: Tumour suppressors such as p53 normally halt the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis. One working allele is usually enough, so both must be lost. A single gain-of-function mutation describes a proto-oncogene becoming an oncogene.

questions.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are guanine?
questions.x: A pairs with T, so T = 30% and A + T = 60%. That leaves 40% for G + C, and G = C, so G = 20%.

questions.q: Bacteria grown for many generations in ¹⁵N are moved to ¹⁴N and allowed to divide twice. What DNA is found after the second division?
o: 50% hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) and 50% light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N)
100% hybrid
25% heavy, 50% hybrid and 25% light
50% heavy and 50% light
questions.x: Replication is semi-conservative. After one division all DNA is hybrid. In the second, each hybrid molecule gives one hybrid and one fully light molecule.

questions.q: Name the enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
questions.x: DNA ligase forms the final phosphodiester bond between adjacent fragments, after the RNA primers have been replaced with DNA.

questions.q: Why is one strand replicated discontinuously, as Okazaki fragments?
o: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end, so it builds new DNA 5′ → 3′, and one strand runs the opposite way to fork movement.
Helicase can only unwind short sections at a time.
The lagging strand template has more introns.
RNA primers can only bind to one strand.
questions.x: The template strands are antiparallel. On one, synthesis 5′ → 3′ follows the fork (leading strand); on the other it runs away from the fork, so it is made in short pieces, each needing a new primer.

questions.q: Why do linear chromosomes get shorter after each round of replication in most somatic cells?
o: When the last RNA primer at the end of the lagging strand is removed, DNA polymerase cannot fill the gap because there is no 3′-OH to extend.
DNA ligase cannot join the leading strand to the telomere.
Helicase cannot unwind the tightly coiled telomere.
Telomerase removes nucleotides from the ends of chromosomes.
questions.x: This is the end-replication problem. Repeated non-coding telomeres act as a buffer so genes aren't lost. Telomerase, active in germ cells and many cancers, adds repeats back rather than removing them.

questions.q: An mRNA codon is 5′-AUG-3′. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
questions.x: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel: A–U, U–A, G–C, reading 3′-UAC-5′ (also written 5′-CAU-3′). RNA has U, not T.

questions.q: Name the enzyme that synthesises mRNA from a DNA template.
questions.x: RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase II for mRNA in eukaryotes) binds the promoter, unwinds the DNA and joins ribonucleotides complementary to the template strand.

questions.q: Which is NOT a modification of eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
o: glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus
adding a 5′ methylguanosine cap
adding a poly(A) tail
splicing out introns
questions.x: Capping, polyadenylation and splicing happen in the nucleus and make mature mRNA. Glycosylation adds sugars to proteins in the ER and Golgi; it doesn't happen to mRNA.

questions.q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon to the stop codon inclusive, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide made?
questions.x: 903 / 3 = 301 codons. The stop codon codes for no amino acid, so 300 amino acids are joined.

questions.q: Why can translation start on an mRNA before its transcription is finished in bacteria, but not in eukaryotes?
o: Bacteria have no nuclear envelope separating transcription from translation.
Bacterial ribosomes are smaller and move faster.
Bacterial mRNA has no start codon.
Bacteria have no RNA polymerase.
questions.x: In bacteria both processes happen in the cytoplasm, so ribosomes attach to the mRNA as it is made. In eukaryotes mRNA is made and processed in the nucleus and must be exported first.

questions.q: Why is inserting one nucleotide near the start of a gene usually more harmful than substituting one nucleotide?
o: It shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it.
It always creates a stop codon at that point.
It changes the gene's promoter.
Insertions can't be repaired, but substitutions always are.
questions.x: Codons are read in triplets with no gaps, so an insertion is a frameshift that alters all downstream amino acids. A substitution changes at most one codon and, since the code is degenerate, may change nothing.

questions.q: What is the mutation that causes sickle cell anaemia?
o: A base substitution in the β-globin gene changes glutamic acid to valine.
A deletion removes the whole β-globin gene.
A frameshift in the α-globin gene creates an early stop codon.
An extra copy of chromosome 11 doubles the amount of β-globin.
questions.x: A single substitution in codon 6 (GAG → GTG on the coding strand) replaces polar glutamic acid with non-polar valine. The new hydrophobic patch makes HbS molecules stick together at low oxygen, distorting red cells.

questions.q: Part of a gene's coding strand reads 5′-ATG GCA TGG AAA-3′. The 9th nucleotide changes from G to A. What type of mutation is this? (Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.)
o: nonsense
silent
missense
frameshift
questions.x: TGG becomes TGA, so the mRNA codon changes from UGG (tryptophan) to UGA, a stop codon. Translation ends early: a nonsense mutation.

questions.q: Three consecutive nucleotides, making up exactly one codon, are deleted from the middle of a gene. What is the most likely result?
o: The polypeptide lacks one amino acid but is otherwise unchanged.
Every amino acid after the deletion is different.
No polypeptide is made at all.
The polypeptide gains one extra amino acid.
questions.x: Removing a whole codon keeps the reading frame, so only one amino acid is lost. The CFTR ΔF508 mutation in cystic fibrosis is an example; even one missing amino acid can stop the protein folding properly.

questions.q: In the lac operon, where does the active repressor protein bind?
o: operator
promoter
lacI gene
lacZ gene
questions.x: The repressor binds the operator, which overlaps the promoter, blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing lacZ, lacY and lacA. lacI is the gene that codes for the repressor.

questions.q: Under which conditions is the lac operon transcribed at the highest rate?
o: lactose present, glucose absent
lactose present, glucose present
lactose absent, glucose absent
lactose absent, glucose present
questions.x: Lactose (as allolactose) removes the repressor. With no glucose, cAMP is high and the CAP–cAMP complex binds near the promoter, strongly increasing transcription.

questions.q: How does tryptophan switch off the trp operon?
o: It binds the inactive repressor and activates it, so the repressor binds the operator.
It binds the active repressor and removes it from the operator.
It binds RNA polymerase directly and inhibits it.
It is broken down to produce cAMP, which blocks the promoter.
questions.x: The trp operon is repressible. Its repressor is made inactive; tryptophan acts as a corepressor that changes its shape so it can bind the operator. The lac operon is the inducible one, where the inducer removes the repressor.

questions.q: A mutation in lacI makes a repressor that can't bind the operator. What happens to the lac structural genes?
o: They are transcribed even when lactose is absent.
They are never transcribed.
They are transcribed only when glucose is present.
They are transcribed only when lactose is present, as normal.
questions.x: Without a repressor on the operator, nothing blocks RNA polymerase, so the genes are expressed constitutively, whether or not lactose is present.

questions.q: A mutation in lacI makes a repressor that still binds the operator but can no longer bind allolactose. What happens when lactose is added and glucose is absent?
o: The structural genes stay switched off.
The structural genes are transcribed at a high rate.
The structural genes are transcribed at a low rate, without CAP.
The repressor is degraded and transcription starts.
questions.x: Allolactose normally changes the repressor's shape so it falls off the operator. If it can't bind, the repressor stays on, so the operon can't be induced even when it would be most useful.

questions.q: Which change makes a eukaryotic gene more likely to be transcribed?
o: acetylation of histones near the gene
methylation of cytosines in the promoter
packing of the region into heterochromatin
removal of transcription factors from the enhancer
questions.x: Acetylation neutralises positive charges on histones, loosening their grip on DNA. The chromatin opens (euchromatin), so transcription factors and RNA polymerase can reach the promoter. The other three all silence genes.

questions.q: An enhancer lies 20 kb upstream of a gene's promoter. How can it increase transcription from so far away?
o: Activator proteins bind the enhancer, the DNA loops, and they help assemble the transcription initiation complex at the promoter.
RNA polymerase starts transcribing at the enhancer and continues to the gene.
The enhancer is transcribed into a protein that acts as a transcription factor.
The enhancer is cut out and inserted next to the promoter.
questions.x: DNA bending brings enhancer-bound activators into contact with mediator proteins and general transcription factors at the promoter, stabilising RNA polymerase binding there.

questions.q: Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed. Tall is dominant. What is the expected ratio of tall to short offspring?
questions.x: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. TT and Tt are both tall, so 3 tall : 1 short. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotype ratio.

questions.q: A plant with the dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant. Half the offspring show the recessive phenotype. What was the genotype of the dominant parent?
o: heterozygous
homozygous dominant
homozygous recessive
It cannot be worked out.
questions.x: In a test cross, Aa × aa gives 1 Aa : 1 aa. A homozygous AA parent would give only dominant offspring.

questions.q: Two plants heterozygous at two unlinked genes (AaBb × AaBb) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is aabb?
questions.x: For independently assorting genes, multiply: P(aa) × P(bb) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

questions.q: Red–green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A carrier woman and a man with normal vision have a son. What is the probability that he is colour-blind?
questions.x: A son always gets his Y from his father and an X from his mother. The mother is XᴮXᵇ, so the son has a 1/2 chance of XᵇY. (1/4 is the chance for any child before knowing its sex.)

questions.q: A dihybrid cross gives an F₂ ratio of 9 : 3 : 4. What does this suggest?
o: recessive epistasis
dominant epistasis
codominance
linked genes
questions.x: The usual 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 becomes 9 : 3 : 4 when a homozygous recessive at one gene (aa) hides the other gene, merging the last two classes (3 + 1). Dominant epistasis typically gives 12 : 3 : 1.

questions.q: A test cross AaBb × aabb gives 42% AB, 42% ab, 8% Ab and 8% aB phenotypes. What is the recombination frequency between the genes?
questions.x: The two large classes are parental; the two small ones are recombinants formed by crossing over. 8% + 8% = 16%, so the genes are linked and about 16 map units apart.

questions.q: A χ² test on a dihybrid cross gives χ² = 2.1 with 3 degrees of freedom. The critical value at p = 0.05 is 7.82. What can be concluded?
o: The difference from the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is not significant and is due to chance.
The difference is significant, so the genes must be linked.
The results prove the genes assort independently.
There are too few degrees of freedom to use the test.
questions.x: 2.1 is below the critical value, so p > 0.05: we accept the null hypothesis that the results fit the expected ratio. A χ² test can't 'prove' a hypothesis, only fail to reject it.

questions.q: A father with blood group A and a mother with blood group B have a child with blood group O. What is the probability that their next child has blood group AB?
questions.x: An O child is IᴼIᴼ, so both parents must be heterozygous: IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ. The chance of Iᴬ from the father and Iᴮ from the mother is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.q: Name the enzyme HIV uses to make DNA from its RNA genome.
questions.x: HIV is a retrovirus. Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy of the RNA genome, and integrase then inserts it into the host chromosome as a provirus.

questions.q: What happens to phage DNA during the lysogenic cycle?
o: It is integrated into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage and copied each time the cell divides.
It is copied many times, and new phages burst out of the cell.
It is broken down by bacterial restriction enzymes.
It is reverse-transcribed into RNA.
questions.x: In lysogeny the phage genome stays dormant within the host chromosome and passes to daughter cells. A trigger can later switch it into the lytic cycle, which ends with lysis.

questions.q: How does antigenic shift produce a new influenza strain?
o: Two different strains infect the same cell and their RNA segments are reassorted into new virus particles.
Point mutations slowly accumulate in the haemagglutinin gene.
The virus integrates into the host genome and picks up human genes.
Antibodies cause the virus to change its surface proteins.
questions.x: Influenza's genome is in 8 separate RNA segments. When two strains (for example avian and human) infect one cell, segments mix, giving sudden major changes in haemagglutinin or neuraminidase. Gradual point mutations are antigenic drift.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections?
o: Viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target.
Viruses are too small for antibiotics to reach.
Viruses quickly break antibiotics down with enzymes.
Viruses live only outside host cells.
questions.x: Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as peptidoglycan walls and 70S ribosomes. Viruses replicate using the host's machinery, so there is nothing for antibiotics to act on.

questions.q: Why can't antiretroviral drugs completely cure an HIV infection?
o: The provirus stays integrated and inactive in long-lived memory T cells, where the drugs can't reach it.
HIV has a DNA genome that the drugs can't recognise.
The drugs kill all helper T cells.
HIV infects only red blood cells.
questions.x: Antiretrovirals block steps such as reverse transcription. A latent provirus isn't using those steps, so it survives and can reactivate if treatment stops.

questions.q: A bacterium transfers a copy of a plasmid to another bacterium through a pilus. What is this process?
o: conjugation
transformation
transduction
binary fission
questions.x: In conjugation, a donor with an F plasmid makes a sex pilus that joins it to a recipient, and DNA passes between them. Transformation is uptake of free DNA; transduction uses a phage.

questions.q: Griffith injected mice with heat-killed virulent S bacteria mixed with live harmless R bacteria. The mice died and live S bacteria were found in them. What process explains this?
o: transformation
conjugation
transduction
mutation of the R bacteria caused by heat
questions.x: The live R bacteria took up DNA released from the dead S bacteria, including the genes for the capsule, and became virulent.

questions.q: Two bacterial strains are kept apart by a filter that lets viruses through but not bacteria. Recombinant bacteria still appear, even after DNase is added. How were genes transferred?
o: transduction
transformation
conjugation
binary fission
questions.x: The filter stops cell contact, ruling out conjugation. DNase would destroy free DNA, ruling out transformation. DNA inside a phage capsid is protected and passes the filter, so transduction is responsible.

questions.q: Where in the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
o: stroma
thylakoid membrane
thylakoid lumen
intermembrane space
questions.x: The Calvin cycle enzymes, including RuBisCO, are in the stroma. The light-dependent reactions happen on the thylakoid membranes.

questions.q: Which products of the light-dependent reactions are used in the Calvin cycle?
o: ATP and reduced NADP
ATP and oxygen
reduced NADP and oxygen
glucose and ATP
questions.x: ATP and reduced NADP are used to reduce GP to triose phosphate, and ATP also regenerates RuBP. Oxygen is a waste product.

questions.q: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, where do the electrons that replace those lost by photosystem II come from?
o: water
reduced NADP
photosystem I
carbon dioxide
questions.x: Photolysis splits water: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The electrons refill PSII, and this is the source of the oxygen released.

questions.q: A plant in bright light suddenly has its CO₂ supply cut off. What happens immediately to RuBP and GP?
o: RuBP rises and GP falls.
RuBP falls and GP rises.
Both rise.
Both fall.
questions.x: Without CO₂, RuBisCO can't fix RuBP into GP, so RuBP builds up. GP is still being converted to triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP, so it falls.

questions.q: During the light-dependent reactions, where are protons concentrated, and where is ATP made?
o: Protons build up in the thylakoid lumen; ATP is made in the stroma.
Protons build up in the stroma; ATP is made in the thylakoid lumen.
Protons build up in the intermembrane space; ATP is made in the matrix.
Protons build up in the cytoplasm; ATP is made in the stroma.
questions.x: The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ into the lumen, and photolysis adds more there. H⁺ flows back out through ATP synthase, which faces the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses the ATP. The intermembrane space and matrix belong to mitochondria.

questions.q: Light is available, but NADP⁺ is in short supply because the Calvin cycle has slowed. Which process continues, and what does it produce?
o: Cyclic photophosphorylation, producing ATP only.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation, producing ATP and reduced NADP.
Photolysis, producing oxygen and reduced NADP.
Cyclic photophosphorylation, producing ATP and oxygen.
questions.x: In cyclic flow, electrons from PSI return to the electron transport chain instead of reducing NADP⁺. This pumps protons and makes ATP, but PSII and photolysis aren't involved, so no reduced NADP or O₂ forms.

questions.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
o: cytoplasm
mitochondrial matrix
inner mitochondrial membrane
intermembrane space
questions.x: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and doesn't need oxygen. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondrial matrix for the link reaction and Krebs cycle.

questions.q: What is the net number of ATP molecules made by substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis, per glucose?
questions.x: 2 ATP are used to phosphorylate glucose and 4 are produced, so the net gain is 2 ATP (plus 2 reduced NAD).

questions.q: How many CO₂ molecules are released by the link reaction and Krebs cycle together, per glucose?
questions.x: Each pyruvate loses 1 CO₂ in the link reaction and 2 in the Krebs cycle. Glucose gives 2 pyruvate, so 2 × 3 = 6, accounting for all six carbon atoms.

questions.q: Cyanide blocks the final enzyme of the electron transport chain. Why does the Krebs cycle also stop?
o: Reduced NAD and FAD can't be oxidised, so no NAD⁺ or FAD is available for the Krebs cycle.
Cyanide binds directly to the Krebs cycle enzymes.
There is no oxygen to react with acetyl CoA.
ATP builds up and inhibits the cycle.
questions.x: With the chain blocked, electrons can't pass to O₂, so reduced NAD and FAD aren't oxidised. The Krebs cycle needs NAD⁺ and FAD as hydrogen acceptors, so it stops too.

questions.q: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the main purpose of this?
o: to regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
to produce extra ATP from pyruvate
to store energy for later use
to provide oxygen for the electron transport chain
questions.x: When O₂ is short, reduced NAD can't be oxidised by the electron transport chain. Reducing pyruvate to lactate oxidises reduced NAD back to NAD⁺, so glycolysis keeps making its 2 ATP. The step itself makes no ATP.

questions.q: An uncoupler makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to H⁺. What happens to oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis?
o: Oxygen uptake continues or rises, but ATP synthesis falls and more energy is released as heat.
Both oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis stop.
Oxygen uptake stops, but ATP synthesis continues.
Both rise.
questions.x: Electron transport, and so O₂ use, continues and may speed up. Protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase, so the gradient's energy is lost as heat instead of making ATP.

questions.q: Name the second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase when glucagon binds its receptor.
questions.x: Activated adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A and starts the cascade leading to glycogen breakdown.

questions.q: What type of receptor does glucagon bind to on liver cells?
o: G protein-coupled receptor
receptor tyrosine kinase
ligand-gated ion channel
intracellular receptor in the nucleus
questions.x: Glucagon binds a GPCR, activating a G protein, then adenylyl cyclase and cAMP. Insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase.

questions.q: How can a tiny amount of glucagon release a large amount of glucose from a liver cell?
o: Each activated enzyme in the cascade activates many molecules of the next, amplifying the signal.
Each glucagon molecule binds thousands of receptors.
Glucagon is converted directly into glucose.
Glucagon enters the cell and is copied.
questions.x: One receptor activates many G proteins; each adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP; each protein kinase phosphorylates many enzymes. The number of active molecules multiplies at each step.

questions.q: What happens straight after insulin binds to its receptor tyrosine kinase?
o: Two receptor subunits come together and phosphorylate each other's tyrosine residues, so relay proteins can bind.
A G protein exchanges GDP for GTP.
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP.
The receptor enters the nucleus and acts as a transcription factor.
questions.x: Ligand binding brings the receptor subunits together and activates their kinase domains, which cross-phosphorylate tyrosines. Phosphotyrosines act as docking sites for relay proteins, eventually moving GLUT4 to the cell surface.

questions.q: A mutation stops the Gα subunit from hydrolysing GTP. A liver cell is exposed to glucagon briefly, then glucagon is removed. What happens?
o: Adenylyl cyclase stays active, so cAMP stays high and glycogen breakdown continues.
Adenylyl cyclase is never activated.
The cell responds normally and stops when glucagon is removed.
Glycogen synthesis increases.
questions.x: Gα switches off by hydrolysing its bound GTP to GDP. If it can't, it stays active even after the hormone leaves, so the response doesn't shut down. Cholera toxin acts in a similar way in gut cells.

questions.q: What is the original source of new alleles in a population?
o: mutation
crossing over
independent assortment
natural selection
questions.x: Only mutation creates new alleles. Crossing over and independent assortment reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations; natural selection changes allele frequencies.

questions.q: Human babies of intermediate birth weight have the highest survival rate. What type of selection is this?
o: stabilising selection
directional selection
disruptive selection
artificial selection
questions.x: Selection against both extremes keeps the mean the same and narrows the range: stabilising selection. Directional shifts the mean; disruptive favours both extremes.

questions.q: Which statement correctly explains how a bacterial population becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
o: A few bacteria already had a resistance allele by chance; the antibiotic kills the others, so resistant ones survive and reproduce.
The antibiotic causes mutations that make the bacteria resistant.
Bacteria become resistant after being exposed to the antibiotic and pass this on.
Bacteria learn to avoid the antibiotic.
questions.x: Mutations arise randomly, before exposure. The antibiotic is the selection pressure: it doesn't cause resistance, it removes susceptible bacteria, so the frequency of the resistance allele rises.

questions.q: A flood kills most of a population at random, and the few survivors have much less genetic diversity. What is this an example of?
o: a bottleneck effect (genetic drift)
the founder effect
directional selection
gene flow
questions.x: A sudden random reduction in population size is a bottleneck, a form of genetic drift: allele frequencies change by chance, not because of fitness. The founder effect is when a small group starts a new population elsewhere.

questions.q: Why does the sickle cell allele stay common in regions where malaria is widespread?
o: Heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria than either homozygote, so both alleles are maintained.
The sickle cell allele is dominant.
Malaria causes the sickle cell mutation.
People with sickle cell anaemia have more children.
questions.x: HbA HbS heterozygotes resist malaria and rarely have severe anaemia, so they have the highest fitness. Selection against both homozygotes (anaemia and malaria) keeps the allele in the population: heterozygote advantage.

questions.q: According to the biological species concept, what is a species?
o: a group of organisms that can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring
a group of organisms that look alike
a group of organisms that live in the same habitat
a group of organisms with identical DNA
questions.x: The biological species concept is based on reproductive isolation. Horses and donkeys can mate but their offspring (mules) are sterile, so they are separate species.

questions.q: A population of beetles is split by a new river. Over time the two groups can no longer interbreed. What kind of speciation is this?
o: allopatric
sympatric
artificial
convergent
questions.x: Allopatric speciation follows geographical isolation. With no gene flow, mutation, selection and drift act separately on each group until they become reproductively isolated.

questions.q: A tetraploid plant arises from a diploid species. Why can it be considered a new species straight away?
o: Crosses with the diploid parent produce triploid offspring, which are sterile.
It is geographically isolated from the parent species.
It cannot carry out photosynthesis.
Tetraploid plants can only reproduce asexually.
questions.x: Gametes from the tetraploid (2n) and the diploid (n) give triploid (3n) offspring whose chromosomes can't pair evenly in meiosis, so they are sterile. Speciation happens in the same place: sympatric speciation.

questions.q: Name the taxonomic rank between class and family.
questions.x: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

questions.q: The number of amino acid differences in cytochrome c between species W and four other species is: P 12, Q 3, R 20, S 8. Which species shares the most recent common ancestor with W?
o: Q
P
R
S
questions.x: Differences accumulate over time after two lineages split, so the fewest differences (3, with Q) means the most recent common ancestor.

questions.q: Which feature do Archaea share with Eukarya but not with Bacteria?
o: DNA associated with histone proteins
70S ribosomes
a circular chromosome
a membrane-bound nucleus
questions.x: Most archaea package DNA with histones, as eukaryotes do; bacteria don't. 70S ribosomes and circular chromosomes are shared by Archaea and Bacteria, and only eukaryotes have a nucleus.

questions.q: Which cells secrete antibodies?
o: plasma cells
memory B cells
helper T cells
macrophages
questions.x: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which have extensive rough ER for secreting antibodies. Memory B cells remain for future responses.

questions.q: Which part of an antibody determines which antigen it binds?
o: the variable regions at the tips of the heavy and light chains
the constant region of the heavy chains
the disulfide bonds joining the chains
the hinge region
questions.x: Each antibody has two antigen-binding sites formed by the variable regions, whose amino acid sequence differs between antibodies. The constant region interacts with phagocytes and complement.

questions.q: A baby receives antibodies from its mother across the placenta. What type of immunity is this?
o: natural passive immunity
natural active immunity
artificial passive immunity
artificial active immunity
questions.x: It is passive because the baby didn't make the antibodies, and natural because no medical treatment was involved. A vaccine gives artificial active immunity.

questions.q: Why is the secondary immune response faster and larger than the primary response?
o: Memory cells made in the first response recognise the antigen and divide quickly.
Antibodies from the first infection stay in the blood for life.
The pathogen is weaker the second time.
Macrophages remember the pathogen.
questions.x: Clonal expansion in the primary response leaves many long-lived memory B and T cells. On re-exposure they respond rapidly, producing more antibody sooner, often before symptoms appear.

questions.q: Why is tuberculosis treated with several antibiotics taken together for at least six months?
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly and hides in macrophages, and using several drugs makes it unlikely that a resistant mutant survives all of them.
Each antibiotic kills only one type of white blood cell.
TB is caused by a virus, so it needs several drugs.
The antibiotics are only effective after six months.
questions.x: Slow growth and survival inside macrophages make the bacteria hard to clear. A bacterium would need resistance to every drug at once to survive, and finishing the full course stops partly resistant survivors from multiplying.

questions.q: Why does HIV infection weaken both antibody (humoral) and cell-mediated responses?
o: HIV destroys helper T cells, which are needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
HIV destroys all B cells directly.
HIV antibodies block every other antibody.
HIV infects red blood cells, reducing oxygen supply to the immune system.
questions.x: HIV infects CD4⁺ helper T cells. Without their cytokines, B cells aren't activated to become plasma cells and cytotoxic T cells aren't activated, so opportunistic infections take hold (AIDS).

questions.q: Why is penicillin most effective against bacteria that are actively growing and dividing?
o: It blocks the cross-linking of new peptidoglycan, so growing cells make weak walls and burst by osmosis.
It blocks bacterial 70S ribosomes, which are only active during division.
It digests the existing cell wall of any bacterium.
It damages bacterial DNA as it replicates.
questions.x: Penicillin inhibits the enzymes (transpeptidases) that cross-link peptidoglycan. Only cells building new wall are affected; their weakened walls can't resist osmotic water entry, so they lyse. Human cells have no walls, so they aren't harmed.

questions.q: Which greenhouse gas is released in the largest amount by burning fossil fuels?
o: carbon dioxide
methane
water vapour
ozone
questions.x: Burning coal, oil and gas oxidises their carbon to CO₂, which is the main driver of human-caused warming.

questions.q: What causes coral bleaching when sea temperatures rise?
o: Corals expel the photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) living in their tissues.
The coral skeleton dissolves.
Corals produce less pigment because there is less light.
Bacteria in warm water digest the coral.
questions.x: Heat stress makes the zooxanthellae produce harmful reactive oxygen species, so the coral expels them. Corals lose their colour and their main food supply, and may starve if the heat continues.

questions.q: How does rising atmospheric CO₂ harm shell-forming marine animals?
o: More CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing the carbonate ions needed to build calcium carbonate shells.
CO₂ is toxic to animals with shells.
CO₂ reduces the amount of oxygen dissolved in seawater.
Warmer water makes calcium carbonate more soluble.
questions.x: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The extra H⁺ reacts with CO₃²⁻ to form more HCO₃⁻, so less carbonate is available for calcification, and acidic water can even dissolve existing shells.

questions.q: Turtle eggs incubated at higher temperatures develop mostly into females. What is a likely effect of warming beaches?
o: sex ratios skewed towards females, which may reduce breeding success
more males, which increases competition
faster hatching with no change in sex ratio
turtles switching to genetic sex determination within one generation
questions.x: In temperature-dependent sex determination, warmer nests produce more females. Too few males can reduce mating success and genetic diversity. Animals can't switch their sex-determination system within a generation.

questions.q: Warmer springs make caterpillars peak earlier, but a bird species still times its breeding by day length. What is the likely result?
o: Chicks hatch after the caterpillar peak and have less food, so fewer survive.
Chicks hatch with more food than before.
Birds start laying eggs earlier, matching the caterpillars.
The caterpillar population falls because more chicks eat them.
questions.x: Day length doesn't change with climate, but temperature-driven events do. This phenological mismatch leaves chicks hatching when food is already declining.

questions.q: Why does rising temperature reduce net photosynthesis in many C3 plants?
o: RuBisCO fixes O₂ instead of CO₂ more often as temperature rises, increasing photorespiration.
Chlorophyll is denatured at temperatures just above 25 °C.
Higher temperatures stop the light-dependent reactions.
Stomata stay fully open, so the plant takes in too much CO₂.
questions.x: As temperature rises, CO₂ becomes less soluble relative to O₂ and RuBisCO's oxygenase activity increases. Photorespiration wastes energy and releases fixed carbon as CO₂, lowering net carbon gain.
